newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia childrens' slaughter pinpoints helplessness.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia childrens' slaughter pinpoints helplessness.

text.p: Svetlana Mitusova lies awake at night shuddering at the thought of the water seeping down her wall from the flat above and wondering if she could have done anything to stop what went on up there.
"I can't sleep...I keep thinking, am I somehow to blame?" she said, her face creasing in anguish.
Mitsova lives in a block of flats called the "cannibals' house" by the people of this Siberian town.
On October 24, police broke into the apartment above Mitusova's on the top floor of the nine-storey concrete building to allow a plumber to check the heating system.
Inside they found a 15-year-old girl suffering from terrible injuries, the corpse of another, aged 13, and a lump of torso which turned out to be the remains of their friend, also 13.
Three days later police found the man who lived in the flat. Alexander Spesivtsev is now in prison facing trial for premeditated murder. His sister and mother are also being held.

"During this year they lured young girls into their apartment, tortured and killed them and then ate them," Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov told a Moscow news conference, praising the police for catching Spesivtsev.

"Four murders involving cannibalism have already been proven. And five more murders are about to be solved. During the searches in the apartment children's clothes and parts of children's bodies were found," he said.
SPESIVTSEV NOT ON POLICE FILES DESPITE EARLIER CHARGES

Valentin Borkov, the regional deputy prosecutor dealing with the case, was much more cautious. He said only three murders had so far been linked and that it was too early to establish whether cannibalism was involved.
The most chilling thing about the case is not the gruesome details of a month's confinement in the flat described to police by the 15-year-old victim Olga Galtseva before she died in hospital.

It is the fact that Spesivtsev, who had spent more than a year in a high-security mental hospital on murder charges after his girlfriend was found dead in 1992, was not on any police lists. He was released in 1994 after which charges against him were dropped because of lack of evidence.
This means that when the dismembered bodies of five children were discovered in the Aba river back in July, nobody checked to see if Spesivtsev could have been involved.
Prosecutors are still not sure. "We have reason to believe that Spesitsev was responsible but the investigation is still going on. We have a lot of hard work still to do," said Borkov.

Then again, when police announced that Olga and her friends Yevgenia Barashkina and Anastasia Burnayeva disappeared on September 24, a month before the grim discovery in the flat, they did not question Spesivtsev.

This is despite the fact that Mitusova says she and her neighbours called the police many times. "They used to make such a noise up there, playing their music really loudly and banging on the pipes," she said.
POLICE INHIBITED BY CONCERN FOR PEOPLE'S PRIVACY
Spesitsev's mother would tell callers that her son was mentally ill and that they should leave them alone.

Sometimes Mitusova thought there was no point in complaining, a fact which now haunts her. "I heard screams back in July, and later on in the summer, but I thought it was just another family row," she said.
Until the heating in the entire block failed, leaving the residents shivering in temperatures well below freezing, police said they had no right to break in to the flat.
The authorities defend themselves by referring to the evils of the communist past.

"In a totalitarian society, all crimes are uncovered. But we live in a democratic society, where human rights are protected. What would happen if the police could break in to any flat?," said local prosecutor Vladimir Kyrochkin.
This attitude is not the only tragic aspect of the case which has its roots in Russia's painful political and economic transition.
Olga, Yevgenia and Anastasia were hospital patients when they were lured to the Spetsivtsev's flat.

A nationwide cash shortage means that many hospitals cannot afford to feed their patients. The girls' parents lived too far away for regular visits so gave them money to fend for themselves. It was during a shopping trip that they disappeared.
CASE SHOWS FATALISTIC ATTITUDE
Such horrific crimes are not exclusive to Russia -- there have been recent cases of mass murder of children in Britain and Belgium.

The difference is that here, instead of a national outcry and loud pledges of extensive inquiries, the authorities have been congratulated for uncovering the crime and feel that there is little they could have done to prevent it.
"The law enforcement authorities, if they are guilty, then it is not because they did not uncover it but because they were objectively unable to," said Kurochkin.
"Only Sherlock Holmes uncovers all crimes," he said, when asked why Spesivtsev was let free after the first murder.
"We had enough evidence to suspect him, but not enough to convict him. We have such an understanding of innocent until proven guilty.

"After he was released from hospital he escaped the authorities' attention," explained Borkov. "We will be looking into all aspects of the case, but there is a lot to go through and the investigation may take more than a year. Only then will we be able to say if anyone is to blame."

The people of Novokuznetsk, a heavily-industrialised Siberian town used by both the tsars and their communist successors as a place of exile for criminals, have protested at the crime, but have other worries on their minds.
Many have not been paid for months so outrage at the deaths has been swept up in the everyday struggle to survive.
Mitusova cannot even contemplate moving out of her flat for the simple reason that there is nowhere to go.
